prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, in which designed small molecules recruit ubiquitin ligases to eliminate chosen proteins

statement.case_for: Having read the opening ballots, I move my support to targeted protein degradation. It is the one candidate that four colleagues placed first and a fifth placed third, and the support comes from members with quite different backgrounds. That breadth matters more to me than my own opening ranking. The chemistry is original and clear. A small molecule is designed to bring a ubiquitin ligase and a target protein together, and the work is rich in ternary-complex cooperativity, linker design and ligand-binding physical organic chemistry. It also corresponds to a new modality in drug discovery that independent laboratories have reproduced. Including Handa's identification of cereblon as the thalidomide target gives the citation both strands of the field, the PROTAC concept and the molecular glue mechanism. I ranked it seventh mainly because I weighted clinical maturity heavily, and no degrader is approved yet. The mechanism is established and the pipeline is deep, so I now regard that concern as less decisive than I first did.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. Crews, Deshaies and Sakamoto introduced PROTACs, Ciulli made the VHL-based platform, and Handa, Ito and Kim worked out cereblon and the glue mechanism. A three-person limit forces us to omit at least one of these strands, and Gray is also a serious candidate. It is also uncertain whether PROTACs and glue degraders count as one discovery or two. The absence of an approved degrader means some of the impact is still forward-looking, and a prize now could look early compared with a delivery technology that has already helped hundreds of millions of people.

responses.point: Linke ranks degradation first with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, and acknowledges that omitting the cereblon/thalidomide glue lineage is a real allocation problem.
responses.response: I share the worry about the glue lineage, and I come down differently on how to resolve it. Ciulli's structural and ternary-complex work is a strong contribution, but it refines a platform whose concept Crews and Deshaies had already established. Handa's cereblon identification is a separate mechanistic discovery that explains an existing drug and opens the molecular-glue half of the field. I therefore prefer Handa to Ciulli in the third seat, and I would keep Ciulli as the most likely substitute if the committee judges the drug-like platform more decisive than the target-identification work.

responses.point: Aili ranks degradation first as a clean induced-proximity idea, ranks phase separation second, and asks whether PROTACs and glues are one discovery or two.
responses.response: I agree that the question is unresolved. I think the unifying idea of induced proximity to the ubiquitin-proteasome system is strong enough to support a single citation with the three names above, and that splitting it into two prize parts would be artificial. I also agree with Aili that condensates are conceptually important and physical-chemical in character. As someone who works on lipid and protein self-assembly, I would still not place it first, because the argument about which cellular assemblies are true phase separation is not settled, and the allocation among Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu and Mittag is hard.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalysed C-N coupling first as a mature, ubiquitous synthetic method with a clean two-person attribution, and ranks degradation only eighth because of its early clinical stage.
responses.response: I take the maturity argument seriously, since it was my own reason for ranking degradation low. Buchwald-Hartwig amination has a cleaner attribution and decades of validation, so it is a credible alternative. My reservation is that it extends the cross-coupling chemistry recognised in 2010, whereas degradation introduces a different mode of action. I also think the lack of an approved drug matters less than Somfai suggests. The mechanism is confirmed by many independent groups, and the prize recognises the chemical concept, not a single product. I do not think amination is a better choice than degradation.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks proton-coupled electron transfer first for its conceptual unity across bioenergetics and catalysis, and ranks degradation third.
responses.response: I recognise the conceptual value of PCET, and it is mature and well confirmed. The difficulty I see is attribution. Nocera, Mayer, Hammes-Schiffer and Meyer each contributed, and the field has no single discovery that a short citation can capture, which makes a three-person selection hard to defend. Degradation has a clear stated achievement and a clearer link to the field of chemistry. I would put PCET in a strong second group, but I would not make it the preferred prize.

uncertainties: Whether Handa or Ciulli (or Gray) should take the third seat, and whether Sakamoto is left out unfairly.
Whether the committee treats PROTACs and molecular glues as one achievement or two.
How much weight the lack of an approved degrader drug should carry for timing.
Whether the ionizable lipid nanoparticle carrier, which I ranked first, should be recognised in its own right given the credit spread among Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer.
statement.conflict_note: I work at Lund University in physical chemistry, which is the same institution as Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and I have research overlap with Daniel Aili and Peter Brzezinski on membranes and self-assembly. These are collegial connections and I do not consider them recusal-level. I have no apparent personal or institutional tie to the PROTAC and degrader candidates, to Hiroshi Handa, Craig M. Crews or Raymond J. Deshaies. My own field is lipid self-assembly, which is close to the ionizable lipid nanoparticle and phase separation candidates, and I flag that in case colleagues think it affects how I judge those entries.
